archetype.name: Playoff Team (ground-and-defense)
archetype.definition: A team that wins by running the ball efficiently, owning the clock and holding opponents out of the end zone, with a record a notch ahead of what its underlying play would earn on its own.

report.headline: A top-tier run game and stingy defense, with a record running slightly ahead.
report.take:
Pittsburgh is 6-2 and tied with Cincinnati atop the AFC North. The way it got there is old-fashioned. The offense ranks 18th in EPA per play, but that average blends two different units. The run game leads the league in rush EPA and is second in yards per carry. The passing game sits 26th. Around that sits a defense that ranks 6th in EPA allowed, is 4th in points allowed and gives up touchdowns on only 37.5% of red-zone trips. Add the second-fewest penalties in the league and a positive turnover margin, and you have a team that rarely beats itself and makes opponents earn every point.

The record still flatters the play a little. The point differential implies about 4.4 wins, not six. Wins over expected sit at +1.6, 8th in the league, and the Steelers have won 80% of their one-score games. On its own that would scream regression. History complicates it: this franchise has posted a positive wins-over-expected number in each of the last six seasons, usually by a similar margin. Closing out tight games with low-mistake football looks like a repeatable trait here, not a coin flip. It is still the thinnest part of the résumé, and it shouldn't be counted on for another full half-season of it.

The numbers hide some tension in how the offense is called. Pittsburgh passes more than the situation predicts (5th in pass rate over expected), even though the dropback game is one of the league's least efficient. Aaron Rodgers holds the ball long (27th in time to throw), and the line ranks 21st in sack rate. The best recent football came when the staff leaned the other way: 148 rushing yards in New Orleans and 200 against Cleveland, with the defense winning the rest. The pass rush has a similar quirk. The Steelers rank 3rd in sacks but only 18th in pressure rate, and eight of those sacks came in one game against the Browns. That gap usually narrows.

Where this goes depends on whether the identity holds. Most of the remaining schedule is soft: Philadelphia, Tennessee, Carolina, Houston and two games with a .444 Baltimore team. A ground-and-defense team with a top-ten defense should bank wins there. The real tests are Cincinnati, Denver and Jacksonville, which is where the shaky passing game and a deep-ball defense that ranks 23rd in EPA allowed get exposed.

strengths.title: League's most efficient rushing attack
strengths.body: The Steelers lead the NFL in rush EPA and run success holds up underneath it. They are 2nd in yards per carry and convert 93% of short-yardage runs, best in the league. Yards before contact are only middle of the pack, which points to backs and scheme creating as much as the line. That kind of production tends to travel, and it has been trending up, peaking in the 200-yard game against Cleveland.

strengths.title: Defense that closes the door
strengths.body: The defense is 6th in EPA allowed and 6th against the run. Where it really separates is in the money downs: 7th on third down and 3rd in red-zone touchdown rate. That is how 18 points a game allowed coexists with a merely average pass defense by yardage. Red-zone rates are volatile, but the run defense and third-down work look sturdy.

strengths.title: Clean, possession-heavy football
strengths.body: The Steelers are 2nd in fewest penalties, 6th in time of possession and plus-five in turnover margin. The offensive line commits the fewest penalties per game in the league. This is the engine behind the close-game record, and the franchise's recent history suggests it is a habit rather than a fluke.

concerns.title: The passing game drags everything down
concerns.body: Pass EPA ranks 26th. The causes are structural: Rodgers holds the ball among the longest in the league and the line ranks 21st in sack rate, with 23 sacks taken. The team still passes more than expected, which spends downs on its weakest unit. Michael Pittman Jr.'s eventual return from IR would help, but without a clear timeline this looks like a lasting ceiling on the offense.

concerns.title: Record ahead of the point differential
concerns.body: Six wins against a differential that implies about 4.4, an 80% one-score win rate and +1.6 wins over expected all say the results outran the play. The franchise's track record of beating expectations softens this, but net EPA ranks only 11th. Expect some close games to flip.

concerns.title: Vulnerable deep and to tight ends
concerns.body: The defense is strong underneath, 8th on short passes, but ranks 23rd in deep-pass EPA and 22nd in explosive pass rate. It also allows the 3rd-highest EPA per target to opposing lead tight ends. Sack totals inflated by one eight-sack day may also come down toward a pressure rate that ranks only 18th. Elite passing offenses have a clear blueprint here.

trend.note: After an ugly 3-20 loss at New England, where passing EPA bottomed out, Pittsburgh has been unbeaten since the short-week loss in Cleveland. The run game and defense have both peaked in the last two games, capped by a 27-6 rout with 200 rushing yards and eight sacks.

nextGame.headline: Run at a soft front, keep Burrow on the sideline.
nextGame.body:
This is a first-place showdown and a contrast in styles. Cincinnati has the league's most pass-happy offense, ranking 1st in pass rate over expected and 2nd in pass EPA. Its defense is the weak half: 27th against the run, 30th on third down and 25th on short passes. Pittsburgh won the first meeting 30-27 as a home underdog, in what was easily its best passing game of the year. It now goes on the road as a 3.5-point underdog in a game with a 48.5 total, higher than any Steelers game so far. The Steelers come off a bye with two weeks of rest.

On availability, Pittsburgh is still without WR Michael Pittman Jr. (IR, no firm timeline), and depth corners Brandin Echols and Doneiko Slaughter are out against a pass-first offense. Cincinnati has lost edge rusher Cashius Howell to IR and tight end Erick All Jr. for the season. WR Andrei Iosivas could return from IR, and safety Kyle Dugger is out.

waysToWin.title: Pound the league's worst-tier run defense
waysToWin.body: The NFL's most efficient rushing offense faces a defense ranked 27th against the run, and a run game that dominates also keeps a pass-first offense off the field. Long drives of handoffs shorten the game, keep the explosive Bengals offense watching, and play to Pittsburgh's time-of-possession edge.

waysToWin.title: Work the tight ends underneath
waysToWin.body: Cincinnati gives up the 3rd-most production to lead tight ends relative to their averages, and it ranks 25th on short passes while staying strong deep. Freiermuth and Washington have drawn real target volume. A quick, short passing plan also neutralizes a pass rush that ranks 6th in pressure rate.

waysToWin.title: Win in the red zone
waysToWin.body: Pittsburgh is 3rd in red-zone touchdown rate allowed and 6th in EPA allowed overall. Bending between the 20s but turning Bengals drives into field goals is the realistic way to survive a high-powered offense. The first meeting showed a shootout is winnable if the Steelers match touchdowns with stops near the goal line.

waysToLose.title: Burrow hits the deep ball
waysToLose.body: Cincinnati's pass offense ranks 2nd in EPA, and Pittsburgh's defense ranks 23rd in deep-pass EPA and 22nd in explosive pass rate. The Bengals threw for 282 yards in the first meeting. Missing depth corners makes it harder to cover up mistakes.

waysToLose.title: Pressure stalls a slow passing game
waysToLose.body: Cincinnati ranks 6th in pressure rate and 5th in takeaways. Rodgers holds the ball among the longest in the league, and the line ranks 21st in sack rate. Drive-killing sacks or a turnover on a dropback would flip the possession battle Pittsburgh needs to win.

waysToLose.title: Falling behind forces a shootout
waysToLose.body: If Cincinnati scores early, Pittsburgh has to abandon the run and lean on a passing offense that ranks 26th in EPA. Its 31st-ranked fourth-down aggressiveness and 23rd-ranked special teams leave little margin to claw back.

nextGame.watch: Early-down play calling: whether Pittsburgh commits to the run against Cincinnati's 27th-ranked rush defense or drifts back to its pass-heavy tendencies.

restOfSeason.body:
The run game and the defense against the run look real and should carry the Steelers through a back half heavy on losing teams: Philadelphia, Tennessee, Carolina, Houston and Baltimore twice. Expect a winning record over that stretch and a serious division race with Cincinnati. What will likely regress is the margin in close games and a sack total running well ahead of the pressure rate. A couple of tight wins probably become losses, especially against Denver and Jacksonville.

The passing game is the ceiling. Without better protection, or Pittman returning to add a real target, Pittsburgh profiles as a team that wins low-scoring games and struggles when forced to throw. That works against most of the schedule but caps the upside in January.
swingFactors: Pittman's return and the passing game's efficiency
Whether close-game results keep breaking Pittsburgh's way
The two division games with Cincinnati and Baltimore deciding the AFC North

confidence.note: Eight games with a stable quarterback, and the profile matches franchise history, but close-game luck and one outlier sack game blur the defense's true level.
